prize_parts.citation: For the invention and development of the optical lattice clock

statement.case_for: I keep the optical lattice clock (B027) alone as my final position, with Katori and Ye. Reading the full first round did not change the configuration I proposed there. It changed how I weigh the reasons. Six members now prefer it, but I do not count that as evidence. What persuades me is that the case holds when examined from different specialities. Lindroth supplies the atomic-structure check that the magic-wavelength condition and the blackbody shift budget make the 1e-18 claim credible, and Kroll and Mehlig add that independent laboratories (JILA, RIKEN/Tokyo, PTB, NIST, SYRTE) have reproduced and surpassed it, so neither confirmation nor maturity is in question. As an instrument builder I also value an achievement that is inseparable from the device. Katori's magic-wavelength lattice removes Doppler, recoil and differential light shifts for many atoms at once, and Ye's group showed it at the 1e-18 level and used the many-atom ensemble for new measurements. That is a bounded invention with a clear before and after, and the citation can be drawn around the lattice clock itself, not around optical clocks or precision spectroscopy in general. On the chair's questions, I think the lattice clock is distinct from the 2005 comb prize (which gave a way to count optical cycles) and the 2012 prize for single quantum systems (which concerns trapped ions), because neither contains the many-atom magic-wavelength idea. I would not widen the credit to ion clocks, and I would not wait for the redefinition of the second, since the physics is independently established whatever the metrological bodies decide.
statement.case_against: The strongest objection stands and I do not think the discussion has removed it. Ye's group built on comb and ultrastable-laser technology developed by earlier laureates and others, so a reader could see the prize as a third reward for one precision-spectroscopy lineage. Olsson and Danielsson are right that narrow wording reduces this overlap but does not eliminate it. The clock is also an invention, and its largest scientific payoffs (time-dilation tests, varying constants, dark matter, geodesy, a redefined second) are still mostly prospective, so I weigh the scientific-reach argument less than Lindroth does. The credit leaves out ion-clock pioneers, other Sr and Yb lattice groups and ultrastable-laser developers, which is a real attribution cost that Kroll and Danielsson accept and I accept too. Last, I still think IceCube (B041) is the more consequential discovery, since it opened a new observational window. I rank it below the clock only because I cannot defend a two-name credit for it, not because I think the science is weaker.

responses.point: Lindroth argues that the narrow lattice-clock citation answers the comb precedent, that the pending redefinition of the second does not weaken the physics, and that B057 is the leading alternative but should not be traded for the clean B027.
responses.response: I agree on the narrow citation and on the redefinition. I would test her point about the comb with one question: does the citation text avoid any claim that depends on the comb? If it names the lattice clock and the magic-wavelength condition, I think it does. I also take her challenge about IceCube seriously. She is right that I said the supplied pair may not capture the decisive contributors, and I will not walk that back in round 2. Where I still differ is that I do not put the dark-matter and constants searches into the case, because they are not yet results. The case should rest on the invention and the 1e-18 demonstration.

responses.point: Olsson says the 2005 comb prize already covers much of the enabling frequency metrology, that Ye's contribution is partly pushing accuracy rather than a distinct concept, and that being the safe consensus choice is not an argument for being the best.
responses.response: This is the argument against B027 that I take most seriously, and I agree that consensus is not merit. I think the answer is in the division of the two names, and the committee should state it in the discussion. Katori holds the concept and first demonstration, which is the new idea. Ye's group went beyond an accuracy increment, because the 1e-18 stability needed the many-atom ensemble and the spin-polarised Fermi-gas operation, and that showed what the concept could do. If members think Ye's contribution is only accuracy, then the right outcome is a narrower citation, not a different candidate. I also note that Olsson says she would not insist on B053 if the clock is judged stronger. I would still keep B053 off the ballot as an enabling instrument with an unsettled credit.

responses.point: Eriksson prefers B057 with a citation built on the Z2 classification and the observation of the quantum spin Hall state, argues that the 2016 prize covered a different concept, and says he would defer to me and Danielsson on whether Halzen and Karle are the decisive pair for IceCube.
responses.response: His argument that 2016 concerned the Thouless-Haldane-Kosterlitz framework while the Z2 insulator is a later and distinct concept is persuasive, and I withdraw any suggestion that the overlap alone rules B057 out. My reservation is the credit. A citation built on Z2 and the HgTe observation avoids naming who proposed HgTe as the platform, but Bernevig and Hughes would still be omitted from a prize that mentions HgTe, and the 3D work is left out. On his deferral about IceCube, I do not claim that I can settle it as an astroparticle member. I have no documented tie to the IceCube credited names, but my field proximity means my view of Halzen and Karle should be discounted accordingly. I cannot give him a clean answer, and for that reason I do not put B041 in my configuration.

responses.point: Danielsson ranks B041 third, calls it the most serious competing case, says source associations are statistically less mature than the diffuse flux, and says narrow framing of the clock does not remove the comb overlap but the committee should say so openly.
responses.response: I agree with both points. The diffuse flux is secure, the source associations are less mature, and the credit problem remains for a collaboration that grew from AMANDA. I do not claim a stronger case for B041 than he does. I keep it as an alternative because a discovery of this kind should be revisited if the committee can find a credit that holds. On the comb overlap, I agree that the discussion should record that the lattice clock relies on technology honoured in 2005, and that the committee treats this as acceptable because the lattice clock is a new concept built on that toolkit. I would put that statement in the committee record so the citation is not read as claiming more than it does.

responses.point: Kroll argues against widening the prize to ion clocks, accepts the attribution cost, and says the comb and ion-trap prizes honoured different inventions that do not contain the magic-wavelength lattice.
responses.response: I agree and I have moved to his position on ion clocks. In round 1 I listed the omitted ion-clock and Sr/Yb groups as an uncertainty. I now think a wider credit would force the committee to adjudicate between neutral-atom and ion clocks, and would exceed three people or make the citation vague. The attribution cost is real, but it is a reason to word the citation narrowly, not to add names. I do not see a way to add a second part, such as B032 atom interferometry, within three people, so B027 stands alone.

responses.point: Mehlig asks whether the pending redefinition of the second argues for waiting or for acting now, and he prefers a citation written in terms of the invention and not its applications.
responses.response: I would act now, for the reason he implies. The redefinition is a decision of the metrological community, and a Nobel citation should not wait on it or be written to depend on it. The physics result already stands, with several laboratories agreeing near 1e-18. I agree that the citation should say 'invention and development of the optical lattice clock' and avoid naming the redefinition, dark matter or constants, so that the prize does not commit to outcomes that are not yet established.

uncertainties: Whether the committee accepts that the lattice clock is a new concept built on comb and ultrastable-laser technology honoured earlier, or judges it a further reward for the same lineage
Whether leaving out ion-clock pioneers, early Sr and Yb lattice groups and ultrastable-laser developers is an acceptable cost of a two-name credit
Whether a defensible credit for IceCube exists, and whether my view of Halzen and Karle can be given any weight given my field proximity
Whether the Z2 and HgTe citation for B057 can withstand the omission of Bernevig, Hughes, Zhang and the 3D work; I have not settled this and it remains my second alternative
I recall clock performance figures and priority dates from memory and have not checked them against sources at this stage
statement.conflict_note: As Chair and an astroparticle experimentalist I disclose a field bias toward B041 (IceCube), where I have no documented collaboration or personal tie to Halzen, Karle or the collaboration, but my profile lists PAMELA, Fermi-LAT, PoGOLite/PoGO+ and XL-Calibur. For B027 I have no documented tie to Katori or Ye and no conflict requiring recusal. Several members disclosed proximity to their own candidates (Olsson for B053, Johansson for B036, Eriksson, Lindroth, Kroll and Mehlig for neighbouring fields). I think these call for weighing their positions accordingly, not for recusal, since none of them has a documented tie to a credited person and none of those candidates is in my preferred configuration. I have nothing new to add since round 1.
